findings.text: Queue creation and removal enter through namespace scoped wrappers. Creation optionally copies a user attribute block and delegates to a shared open worker with either a valid pointer or null. Removal resolves the given name under the caller mount root, takes write protection, looks up the target for removal, holds an inode reference across the filesystem unlink, then releases the reference and protection and returns the resulting status.

Native timed send and receive accept an optional absolute timeout address. When present a shared timeout helper translates and validates it with failures returned immediately. When absent a null deadline is used. Both then call a dedicated internal worker carrying descriptor payload location length and priority information.

Thirty two bit timeout variants accept old layout addresses and translate them with a compat helper that reports unreadable memory as EFAULT and invalid normalized times as EINVAL. On success the normalized deadline is forwarded to the same internal timed send or receive worker used by the native path, otherwise the error is returned.

Compat queue control translates narrow user layouts before delegating. Creation translates attributes only when O_CREAT is present. Notification translates a compat event with access and field checks and adjusts the thread cookie pointer from its integer form for SIGEV_THREAD. Attribute query and update use paired attribute converters in both directions and propagate conversion faults.

Native notification and attribute entry points copy user structures and delegate. Notification forwards null as disarm and otherwise forwards the copied event. Attribute control forms optional input and output pointers from user address presence, invokes the shared worker, and on success copies the output block back only when requested.

Payload transfer helpers move bytes between user space and a chained kernel message with a leading area plus extension segments. Loading allocates the chain, copies leading bytes then each segment in order, runs a security hook, and frees everything on copy fault or hook failure with ENOMEM for allocation failure and EFAULT for copy failure. Storing copies the chain out in the same order and reports failure as negative one with zero for success.

Message queue resolution helpers map an integer identifier to a queue object through the per namespace table selected by msg_ids. One form returns the object directly while the other additionally checks the embedded sequence generation against the identifier and rejects mismatches as invalid. Missing slots are also reported as invalid through error pointers.

Lifecycle helpers cover teardown and setup. Queue removal forwards to generic identifier teardown. Namespace setup initializes accounting and default limits then creates and stores a private mount, propagating creation failure. Compat event fetching checks accessibility and copies value signal notify and thread fields individually with fault reporting.

System V queue block begins with a generic permission object, then stamps for last send receive and change, occupancy in bytes, message count, byte capacity, and identifiers for last sender and receiver processes. It ends with three list anchors for messages and for waiting receivers and senders, with layout randomization applied.
Waiting receiver record links into the queue list and stores the sleeping task, a selection mode, a requested type, a size limit, and a slot that will hold the delivered message.
Waiting sender record links into the queue list and stores the sleeping task together with the size of the pending payload.

Compat attribute block holds flags, maximum count, maximum size, and current count as compat longs in that order, followed by four reserved compat longs. Input conversion zeroes a native block then copies the four meaningful fields. Output conversion zeroes a compat block then copies the same four fields back, with copy faults reported.

Message queue filesystem wires fixed operation tables. Directory operations cover lookup creation and removal. File operations cover flush poll read and standard seek. Superblock operations cover inode allocation release eviction and generic filesystem status. Context operations cover release and tree construction. The registered type uses a fixed name, user namespace mount support, and anonymous superblock teardown.

Timed send rejects priority at or above MQ_PRIO_MAX, unknown descriptors, wrong file operations, missing FMODE_WRITE, and lengths above the queue maximum size. It allocates the chained message and tags length and priority before locking, and speculatively allocates a tree leaf only when the spare cache is empty. Under lock a full queue fails with EAGAIN for O_NONBLOCK or sleeps with the message attached, while a non full queue either hands the message directly to the first receiver or inserts it with notification and timestamp refresh. Insertion or sleep failure frees the message.

Timed receive rejects unknown descriptors, wrong file operations, missing FMODE_READ, and caller buffers smaller than the queue maximum size. It speculatively allocates a spare tree leaf only when the cache is empty. Under lock an empty queue fails with EAGAIN for O_NONBLOCK or sleeps and adopts the message supplied later, while a nonempty queue extracts one message, refreshes timestamps, and either admits the first sender or wakes poll waiters. After unlock priority and payload are copied out and the message is freed, with copy faults reported as EFAULT.

Notification setup allows only SIGEV_NONE SIGEV_SIGNAL and SIGEV_THREAD and validates signal numbers. Thread mode allocates a fixed cookie packet, copies the cookie from user space, looks up the netlink socket named by the signal field, and attaches the packet with retry on race. Under lock null clears registration only for the owning thread group, duplicate registration fails with EBUSY, otherwise the chosen mode is stored with signal details or socket and cookie as appropriate, owner group and user namespace are captured, execution identity is captured for signal delivery, and timestamps are refreshed.

Attribute control rejects input flags containing bits beyond O_NONBLOCK. Under lock an output request receives stored attributes with flags synthesized from the file nonblocking state. An update audits the request then sets or clears only the nonblocking file flag under a nested file lock and refreshes timestamps, leaving maximum count size and current count unchanged.

Identifier decoding masks the low bits for the table index and shifts for the sequence generation. Lookup reports EINVAL for absent slots. Checked lookup additionally compares the stored sequence and reports EINVAL on mismatch. Teardown removes the table slot and, unless the key is IPC_PRIVATE, the hash node, decrements usage, marks deletion, and when the removed index was the cached maximum recomputes it by probing the table from high to low.

Namespace initialization zeroes the queue count, installs defaults for maximum queues messages and sizes from named DFLT constants, creates a private mount, and stores it in the namespace. Filesystem initialization creates a dedicated inode cache with alignment and accounting, registers controls and the filesystem type, initializes a global lock, and initializes the initial namespace, unwinding through unregistration control retirement and cache destruction on failure.

Message allocation sizes the first chunk to the smaller of total length and leading capacity, then appends segments sized to the smaller of remainder and segment capacity, yielding between segments and freeing the partial chain on failure. Security state starts null and is established after payload bytes are copied.

Per inode queue lock protects attributes and counts, the spare node cache, sender and receiver lists, and notification registration. Send receive and notify hold it across inspection mutation and waiter selection, publish waiter readiness with release ordering while holding it, and drain deferred wakeups only after release. Attribute update nests the file flag lock inside the queue lock. Unlink relies on mount write protection rather than the queue lock.

Direct handoff transitions a waiter from queued to ready. The waiter leaves its list, a task reference is held, readiness is published, and the task joins a deferred wake queue. Send applies this to the first receiver with the fresh message attached. Receive applies this to the first sender after freeing space, inserting its message and waking it, or wakes generic poll waiters when no sender waits.

Blocking paths initialize a waiter for the current task in the none state, attaching the outbound message for send, then sleep with an optional deadline while releasing the queue lock. The returned status decides success or failure, with failure freeing the outbound message for send and success adopting the delivered message for receive.
Message selection codes are fixed integers with any one, equal two, not equal three, less equal four, and numeric five.
Compat attribute layout fixes four trailing reserved slots that are ignored on input and zeroed on output.

Failures use standard negative codes. Unreadable or unwritable user memory reports EFAULT. Unknown descriptor, wrong file operations, or missing read or write mode reports EBADF. Oversize send or undersize receive buffer reports EMSGSIZE. Out of range priority, invalid compat timeout, invalid notify mode or signal, and unexpected attribute flags report EINVAL. Full send or empty receive on nonblocking files reports EAGAIN. Duplicate notification reports EBUSY. Message packet or cache allocation failure reports ENOMEM, with netlink lookup errors propagated unchanged.

Speculative leaves are installed only into an empty spare cache and otherwise freed, with missing leaves tolerated through fallback allocation. Fresh messages are freed on insertion failure, sleep failure, or nonblocking full. Extracted messages are freed after copy out even when copy faults. Cookie packets are freed on copy or lookup failure, and socket state is detached when descriptor validation fails after attachment. Unlink keeps the target inode pinned across the filesystem operation. Identifier teardown warns when table or hash removal does not match expectations.
